title: Joining Complex Assemblies
objective: Explain, at knowledge level, the concepts and principles of complex assemblies, how controlled drawings and specifications communicate requirements, and how assembling, fastening, lay-out and fit concepts relate to approved work without providing unsupervised fabrication or joining procedures.

verified_topic_elements: KT0301 — Concepts and principles of joining complex assemblies — 30%
KT0302 — Assembling and fastening methods for complex assemblies — 40%
KT0303 — Lay-out and fit complex assemblies — 30%
internal_assessment_criteria: IAC0301 — Describe the concepts and principles of joining complex assemblies — 30%
IAC0302 — Interpret information from drawings and specifications of complex assemblies and apply relevant knowledge-level calculations — 40%
IAC0303 — Identify, discuss and illustrate assembling and fastening methods for complex assemblies — 30%
curriculum_traceability.primary_source: QCTO occupational curriculum hosted by CHIETA — Curriculum-6.pdf

safety_boundary: Knowledge learning only. This lesson does not authorise fabrication, welding, cutting, powered-tool use, structural modification, lifting or other hazardous practical assembly work. Physical assembly and joining belong in approved occupational training or workplace processes under applicable controls and competent human supervision.

sections.heading: 1. What makes an assembly complex?
sections.body: A complex assembly combines multiple components, relationships and controlled requirements that must be understood together. At knowledge level, the learner focuses on recognising how components relate to the approved assembly information rather than attempting physical fabrication.

sections.heading: 2. Concepts and principles
sections.body: Complex assemblies depend on controlled requirements such as component identity, orientation, relationships, dimensions, references and specified joining requirements. The learner should understand these concepts and explain why assumptions must not replace approved information.

sections.heading: 3. Drawings and specifications
sections.body: Drawings and specifications communicate the approved assembly requirements. Learners should practise interpreting component relationships, dimensions, references and other controlled information and use only calculations appropriate to the approved knowledge-learning context. Unclear or missing information must be referred to the competent trainer or supervisor.

sections.heading: 4. Assembling and fastening concepts
sections.body: The curriculum requires learners to identify, discuss and illustrate assembling and fastening methods for complex assemblies. In this Companion this remains conceptual: learners recognise method categories, purpose and relationships to controlled requirements. Selection, setup and physical use of equipment remain supervised practical competencies.

sections.heading: 5. Lay-out concepts
sections.body: Lay-out establishes how required information is represented and related before components are assembled. At knowledge level, learners should understand the importance of controlled dimensions, references and component relationships. This lesson does not provide operational marking-out or tool-use procedures.

sections.heading: 6. Fit concepts
sections.body: Fit concerns whether components and their relationships conform to the approved assembly requirement. Learners should understand that conformity is checked against controlled information rather than guesswork. Physical adjustment or modification remains part of supervised practical training.

sections.heading: 7. Safe illustration and explanation
sections.body: Learners may use simple diagrams or freehand sketches to communicate assembly concepts at knowledge level. Such representations explain understanding only; they are not fabrication instructions, design approvals or authorisation to perform practical work.

sections.heading: 8. The learning boundary
sections.body: Understanding complex-assembly concepts, drawings, specifications, assembling, fastening, lay-out and fit does not establish practical occupational competence. The Companion prepares learners for supervised training and formal assessment processes; it does not certify or authorise hazardous practical assembly work.

media.title: Working Drawings and Assemblies
media.focus: University theory reference explaining assembly drawings, subassemblies, component identification, parts lists and how drawing views communicate relationships between parts.
media.safety_scope: Theory and drawing interpretation only. Use this resource to understand how components and subassemblies are represented and related in controlled drawings. It does not authorise fabrication, joining, equipment use or other practical assembly work.
